rows.n: Poké Lid — Arcanine, Tenbusu Plaza, Kokusai-dōri (ポケふた ウインディ てんぶす広場)
rows.nat: ポケふた ウインディ てんぶす広場
rows.w: Naha's original Pokémon manhole cover, an Arcanine design on the OCVB 'Flying Pikachu' Poké Lid trail, set in Tenbusu Plaza on Kokusai-dōri. In April 2026 a photo of it covered by pipe chairs during an event drew more than 24 million views. Naha City then said it was considering moving the lid and was in talks with The Pokémon Company. Check it is still here before you go.

rows.n: Pokémon Center Okinawa, Aeon Mall Okinawa Rycom (ポケモンセンターオキナワ)
rows.nat: ポケモンセンターオキナワ
rows.w: Okinawa's first Pokémon Center (opened 11 Aug 2022, Japan's 16th), themed on the island's nature: Pikachu and Arcanine greet you at the entrance, with Okinawa-only goods and a video zone. Pair it with a hunt for the prefecture's 16 Pokémon manhole 'Poké Lids'.

rows.n: Poké Lid — Growlithe over Mihama fireworks, Depot Island Boardwalk, Chatan (ポケふた ガーディ 北谷町美浜)
rows.nat: ポケふた ガーディ 北谷町美浜
rows.w: A Pokémon manhole cover installed in August 2025 at the seaside boardwalk of Depot Island in Mihama. It shows Growlithe, Okinawa's 'support Pokémon', against American Village's night skyline and fireworks. It sits just before the boardwalk steps, which is also a popular fireworks-viewing spot. It is one of four Growlithe lids the Pokémon Company gave to Okinawan towns in 2025.

rows.n: Okitsura pilgrimage — Gushikawa, Uruma (沖ツラ聖地 具志川公民館・具志川ビーチ)
rows.nat: 沖ツラ聖地 具志川公民館・具志川ビーチ
rows.w: The residential Gushikawa district of Uruma is the main real-world setting of the anime 'Fall in Love with Okinawa Dialect' (沖ツラ). Gushikawa Beach appears in episode 2 and other walk-to-school scenes, and pilgrims start from the Gushikawa Community Hall, which hands out Uruma's official location map and has one of three Okitsura manhole covers (the others are at KIN Sunrise Beach and Michi-no-Eki Ginoza).

rows.n: Nishihara Kira Kira Beach (西原きらきらビーチ)
rows.w: A 550 m man-made beach inside Creed Nishihara Marine Park on the east coast, with free entry and parking, sports fields, a barbecue area and beach-volleyball courts. It is the venue of the climactic tournament in the beach-volleyball anime 'Harukana Receive' (2018).

rows.n: Chiikawa Restaurant Okinawa, PARCO CITY Urasoe (ちいかわレストラン 沖縄店)
rows.nat: ちいかわレストラン 沖縄店
rows.w: The second permanent Chiikawa Restaurant in Japan after Ikebukuro PARCO, a family-restaurant-style character café that opened on 13 February 2026 inside San-A Urasoe Nishi-Kaigan PARCO CITY. Alongside the shared grand menu it serves Okinawa-only dishes: the 'sunburnt shīsā' taco rice, a 'mensōre' banana split and a shīsā sanpin-tea tropical drink.

rows.n: Poké Lid — Solrock & Skiploom, Kumiodori Park, Urasoe (ポケふた ソルロック×ポポッコ 組踊公園)
rows.nat: ポケふた ソルロック×ポポッコ 組踊公園
rows.w: Urasoe's Pokémon manhole cover was set into Kumiodori Park, next to the National Theatre Okinawa, in February 2022. That made Urasoe the fifth city in the prefecture with a Poké Lid. Solrock stands for the sun (tida), Urasoe's symbol, and Skiploom carries yellow flowers in the colour of the city flower. It is on the OCVB 'Flying Pikachu' Poké Lid trail.

rows.n: Poké Lid — Tauros & Katsuren Castle, Ishikawa Sports Grounds, Uruma (ポケふた ケンタロス×勝連城跡 石川運動広場)
rows.nat: ポケふた ケンタロス×勝連城跡 石川運動広場
rows.w: Uruma's Pokémon manhole cover shows a charging Tauros, a nod to the city's bullfighting (tōgyū) culture, with the UNESCO-listed Katsuren Castle ruins behind it. It was installed at the entrance of the Ishikawa Sports Grounds as part of Pokémon's 'Flying Pikachu Project' and is on the OCVB Poké Lid trail.

rows.n: Cape Chinen Park (知念岬公園)
rows.w: A grassy clifftop park at the tip of Chinen Cape, about 40 m above the sea, with a roughly 250-degree view over the reef toward Kudaka and Komaka islands, a short walk from Sefa-utaki. It is one of the settings of the 2021 anime 'The Aquatope on White Sand', the reason the Anime Tourism Association named Nanjō one of its '88 Anime Pilgrimage' sites.
ph: Photo: そらみみ · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.n: Poké Lid — Wartortle & Sandygast, Michi-no-Eki Itoman (ポケふた カメール×スナバァ 道の駅いとまん)
rows.nat: ポケふた カメール×スナバァ 道の駅いとまん
rows.w: A Pokémon manhole cover showing Wartortle and Sandygast on an Itoman sandy beach. It is set inside the covered eating area of Michi-no-Eki Itoman, the roadside station that houses the fishermen's co-op fish market. It is one of three south-Okinawa lids unveiled together for Itoman, Tomigusuku and Nanjō, and is on the OCVB Poké Lid trail.

rows.n: Azama Sun Sun Beach (あざまサンサンビーチ)
rows.nat: あざまサンサンビーチ
rows.w: Shallow family beach by Azama port (the ferry to Kudaka), fringed with lawns, with a beach house and reservable BBQ sets.
ph: Photo: そらみみ · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.n: Nirai Kanai Bridge overlook (ニライカナイ橋)
rows.w: A sweeping U-shaped road bridge that switchbacks down the Chinen hillside with the Pacific and Kudaka Island ahead — best seen from the tunnel-top viewpoint. It appears in the 2021 anime 'The Aquatope on White Sand', which earned Nanjō a place among the Anime Tourism Association's 88 anime pilgrimage sites.
ph: Photo: Kugel~commonswiki · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows: 122 places · the top tier, graded within each area

rows.n: Shikinaen Royal Garden (識名園)
rows.w: The Ryūkyū royal family’s largest villa garden, built around a pond with jagged coral-limestone bridges two kilometres south of Shuri Castle; used to receive Chinese envoys and now a UNESCO component.

rows.n: Urizun (古酒と琉球料理 うりずん)
rows.nat: 古酒と琉球料理 うりずん
rows.w: Opened 15 August 1972 by gathering bottles from every awamori distillery in Okinawa — the bar that brought awamori back to the people. Order duru-ten, the fried taro croquette Okinawa Times traces to this kitchen, and a flight of kūsu (aged awamori).

rows.n: Tamaudun Royal Mausoleum (玉陵)
rows.w: Limestone tomb of the second Shō dynasty, built in 1501 under King Shō Shin and modelled on Shuri Castle, its balustrades carved with dragons, phoenixes and lions. A National Treasure as well as a UNESCO component.
ph: Photo: xiquinhosilva · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.n: Tsuboya Yachimun-dōri pottery street (壺屋やちむん通り)
rows.w: The Ryūkyū Kingdom's ceramics quarter: a 400 m stone-paved street between Kokusai-dōri and Route 330 lined with potteries, kilns and shops selling yachimun ware and shisa, with wheel-throwing classes.

rows.n: Kokusai-dōri (国際通り)
rows.w: Naha's 1.6 km main street of shops, cafés, bars and awamori stores, rebuilt so fast after 1945 it was nicknamed the 'Miracle Mile'; the gateway to Makishi market, Tsuboya and the arcades, and the stage for the city's big festivals.
ph: Kokusai-dori street in Naha by day

rows.n: Shuri Soba (首里そば)
rows.w: Lunch-only Shuri shop carrying on the noodle technique of a vanished Shuri original: unbleached flour pressed and rested over two days, a single soba on the menu, queues from before opening and sold out early.

rows.n: Mendokoro Tiandaa (麺処 てぃあんだー)
rows.nat: 麺処 てぃあんだー
rows.w: Cult Naha soba shop known for house-made noodles; the fūchibā soba arrives fragrant with Okinawan mugwort. In both Okinawa Traveler's soba feature and Mapple's Okinawa-soba round-up.

rows.n: Karakara to Chibugwā (カラカラとちぶぐゎ〜)
rows.w: Naha's awamori-specialist bar: bottles from every distillery in the prefecture and aged kūsu past thirty years, with three awamori sommeliers to steer you; prefecture-certified for Ryukyu cuisine.

rows.n: Kozakura (小桜)
rows.w: A seventy-year-old koryōriya off Kokusai-dōri, believed to be the oldest surviving restaurant of its era in Naha; the third-generation owner keeps both old and new Okinawan dishes on the menu.

rows.n: Keishoku no Mise Ruby, Tomari (軽食の店ルビー)
rows.w: Sixty-plus-year-old Tomari diner whose name belies mountainous portions: some 80 dishes from champuru to loco moco, but half the room orders the C-lunch. Namie Amuro used to drop in after dance practice.

rows.n: Fujiya Tomari Honten (富士家 泊本店)
rows.w: The name many Okinawans give first for zenzai: fluffy shaved ice frozen from the bean-cooking syrup so it never dilutes, heaped over sweet kintoki beans. Open daily, later hours in summer.

rows.n: Kokusai-dōri Yatai-mura (国際通り屋台村)
rows.w: A food-stall village opened in 2015 just off Kokusai-dōri, with more than 20 counter stalls cooking Okinawan and island dishes from local ingredients — gurukun and parrotfish sushi, Agu pork dumplings, Ishigaki beef — from 11:00. A central stage hosts island songs and dances.

rows.n: Okinawa Daiichi Hotel breakfast (沖縄第一ホテル 薬膳朝食)
rows.nat: 沖縄第一ホテル 薬膳朝食
rows.w: A five-room hotel founded in 1955 whose medicinal-herb breakfast, devised by founder Shimabukuro Yoshiko from her mother's recipes about 40 years ago, uses some 50 ingredients across 20+ Okinawan dishes (about ¥3,300). One of Naha's famous breakfasts; reservation advised.

rows.n: Yūnangi (ゆうなんぎい)
rows.w: Family-run Okinawan restaurant on a side street off Kokusai-dōri, serving home cooking since 1970 under US administration — hard to get a seat, rated among the best Okinawan food in Naha.

rows.n: Ryūkyū Cuisine Mie (琉球料理 美榮)
rows.w: Founded in 1958 to reproduce the Ryūkyū royal court cuisine of Shō Junnan, gourmet son of the last king, in a wooden two-storey ryōtei behind a formal gate in Kumoji.

rows.n: Tomari Iyumachi Fish Market (泊いゆまち)
rows.w: The Okinawa fisheries co-op's market by Tomari Port, where about 70 percent of the catch sold is tuna, delivered unfrozen the day it is landed. Stalls sell sashimi, seafood bowls, shellfish and mozuku to eat on the upstairs terrace.

rows.n: Ryūkyū Ryōri Nuchigafū (琉球料理 ぬちがふぅ)
rows.nat: 琉球料理 ぬちがふぅ
rows.w: An elegant hilltop restaurant above the southern end of Tsuboya pottery street that Lonely Planet singles out for a memorable dinner of Ryūkyū cuisine. It is on Okinawa Prefecture's certified list of restaurants serving authentic Ryūkyū cuisine.

rows.n: Makishi Public Market (第一牧志公設市場)
rows.w: Naha’s kitchen since 1950: 75 ground-floor stalls of spiny lobster, reef fish, pork and island produce, with upstairs restaurants that cook what you buy (mochiage). Reopened in a new building on 19 March 2023.

rows.n: Okinawa Prefectural Museum & Art Museum (沖縄県立博物館・美術館)
rows.nat: 沖縄県立博物館・美術館
rows.w: The prefecture's flagship museum in Shintoshin: Ryūkyū history, nature and crafts from prehistory to the US era, with a modern Okinawan art wing.
ph: Okinawa Prefectural Museum & Art Museum building

rows.n: Bin-nu-utaki / Bengadake Sacred Grove (弁之御嶽・弁ヶ嶽)
rows.w: At 165.7 m the highest point in Naha, about 1 km east of Shuri Castle. In the Ryūkyū Kingdom it was a state place of worship where the king, or his envoy, prayed for his health and the nation's peace; designated a National Historic Site as 'Bin-nu-utaki' on 15 October 2018.

rows.n: Yogi Park cherry blossoms (与儀公園)
rows.w: City park that is Naha's best-known cherry-blossom spot, with more than 400 Kanhizakura (Taiwan cherry) trees. They flower among Japan's earliest, and the Naha Cherry Blossom Festival is held here in early February.

rows.n: Naminoue Shrine (波上宮)
rows.w: Okinawa’s ichinomiya (chief shrine), perched on a coral bluff above Naminoue Beach; long the place where fishermen and sailors prayed for a safe voyage.
ph: Photo: Rickard Törnblad · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons (resized)

rows.n: Fukushū-en Garden (福州園)
rows.w: Walled Chinese garden opened in 1992 for Naha's sister city Fuzhou, built with materials shipped from Fujian — pagoda over a waterfall, ponds and moon gates in old Kume, the Chinese scholars' quarter.

rows.n: Sueyoshi-gū Shrine & Sueyoshi Park (末吉宮)
rows.w: One of the Eight Shrines of the Ryūkyū Kingdom, perched on a forested limestone ridge in Sueyoshi Park; a stone path climbs through jungle to the rebuilt hall — a quiet counterpoint to Shuri Castle.

rows.n: Sōgen-ji Stone Gate (崇元寺石門)
rows.w: The surviving stone gate of the Ryūkyū royal temple founded in 1527, where all who entered — even the king — had to dismount; the temple was destroyed in WWII but the gate was restored and has been an Important Cultural Property since 1972, fronting a small park.

rows.n: Naminoue Beach & Naminoue Umisora Park (波の上ビーチ・波の上うみそら公園)
rows.nat: 波の上ビーチ・波の上うみそら公園
rows.w: Naha's only city beach, sitting below the cliff-top Naminoue Shrine, with free entry and swimming from mid-April to October. The adjoining Umisora Park's enclosed man-made bay is a favourite with people learning to dive.

rows.n: Sugar Loaf Hill (シュガーローフ / 安里52高地)
rows.nat: シュガーローフ / 安里52高地
rows.w: The low hill the US Marines called Sugar Loaf and the Japanese 'Asato Hill 52', locally Kerama-chiiji, was fought over by the 6th Marine Division and the Japanese 32nd Army in May 1945. Today it is the Asato reservoir park beside Omoromachi monorail station, with an inscribed marker amid the new city centre.

rows.n: Okinogū Shrine, Onoyama Park (沖宮)
rows.w: One of the Ryūkyū Hassha, dedicated to Kumano Gongen and long prayed to for safe voyages by tribute ships. Founded beside Naha harbour (per the 1713 Ryūkyū-koku Yuraiki), designated a National Treasure in 1935, destroyed in 1945, re-established in 1961 and moved to Onoyama Park in 1975.

rows.n: Great Akagi Trees of Shuri Kinjō (首里金城の大アカギ)
rows.w: A grove of six huge akagi (Bischofia) trees and one Ryūkyū hackberry behind the Uchikanagusuku shrine just off the Kinjō-chō stone road, designated a national Natural Monument in 1972; the largest is 5.2 m round and 13 m tall. No other such grove of giant akagi survives in a settled area of Okinawa.

rows.n: Tsuboya Yachimun-dōri pottery street (壺屋やちむん通り)
rows.w: The Ryūkyū Kingdom's ceramics quarter: a 400 m stone-paved street between Kokusai-dōri and Route 330 lined with potteries, kilns and shops selling yachimun ware and shisa, with wheel-throwing classes.

rows.n: Kokusai-dōri (国際通り)
rows.w: Naha's 1.6 km main street of shops, cafés, bars and awamori stores, rebuilt so fast after 1945 it was nicknamed the 'Miracle Mile'; the gateway to Makishi market, Tsuboya and the arcades, and the stage for the city's big festivals.
ph: Kokusai-dori street in Naha by day

rows.n: Kinjō-chō Ishidatami-michi stone-paved road (金城町石畳道)
rows.w: About 300 m survive of the c.1522 limestone-paved royal road that ran south from Shuri Castle, winding steeply between old stone walls and red-tiled houses.

rows.n: Kume Shiseibyō Confucius Temple (久米至聖廟)
rows.w: Naha's Confucian temple, a centre of Chinese learning for the Ryūkyū Kingdom since the original was built in 1671–75; its precinct holds the Meirindō, Okinawa's first public school. Rebuilt in Kume in 2013 beside Fukushū-en, on the old Chinese-émigré Kume village.

rows.n: Bin-nu-utaki / Bengadake Sacred Grove (弁之御嶽・弁ヶ嶽)
rows.w: At 165.7 m the highest point in Naha, about 1 km east of Shuri Castle. In the Ryūkyū Kingdom it was a state place of worship where the king, or his envoy, prayed for his health and the nation's peace; designated a National Historic Site as 'Bin-nu-utaki' on 15 October 2018.

rows.n: Asato Hachimangū Shrine (安里八幡宮)
rows.w: One of the Ryūkyū Hassha, founded in the Tianshun era (1457–64) and enshrining Emperor Ōjin, Empress Jingū and Tamayori-hime; the only Hachiman shrine among the eight. A short walk from Asato and Omoromachi stations.

rows.n: Tomari International Cemetery (泊外人墓地)
rows.w: A small walled cemetery on the north bank of Tomari Port holding about 22 foreigners from the 18th to early 20th centuries and some 300 post-war burials, with a monument to Commodore Perry's 1853 landing. Its oldest Western grave, of the British sailor 'WM HARES', is dated 1816.

rows.n: Arakaki Family Residence, Tsuboya (新垣家住宅)
rows.w: The only surviving 18th-century Tsuboya potter's compound — red-tiled main house, workshop, climbing kiln (the former royal 'Higashi-nu-kama') and stone pigsty-toilet — designated an Important Cultural Property in 2002.

rows.n: Heiwa-dōri Shopping Arcade (平和通り商店街)
rows.w: Covered arcade of around 200 shops branching off Kokusai-dōri toward Makishi Public Market, nicknamed the 'labyrinth arcade'. Named 'Peace Street' by public competition in 1951 after the Heiwa-kan cinema at its mouth; a new generation of shop owners has revived it since the 2000s.

rows.n: Yogi Park cherry blossoms (与儀公園)
rows.w: City park that is Naha's best-known cherry-blossom spot, with more than 400 Kanhizakura (Taiwan cherry) trees. They flower among Japan's earliest, and the Naha Cherry Blossom Festival is held here in early February.

rows.n: Shikina-gū Shrine (識名宮)
rows.w: One of the Ryūkyū Hassha, the eight shrines given royal patronage by the Ryūkyū Kingdom, near Shikinaen in Hantagawa. Its origin story centres on a sacred cave, which the shrine opens to visitors on the 1st and 15th of each month.

rows.n: Sakaemachi Market (栄町市場)
rows.w: Showa-era covered market by Asato station: groceries by day, and after dark a warren of tiny bars and izakaya where locals drink on stools in the alleys.

rows.n: Shikinaen Royal Garden (識名園)
rows.w: The Ryūkyū royal family’s largest villa garden, built around a pond with jagged coral-limestone bridges two kilometres south of Shuri Castle; used to receive Chinese envoys and now a UNESCO component.

rows.n: Tamaudun Royal Mausoleum (玉陵)
rows.w: Limestone tomb of the second Shō dynasty, built in 1501 under King Shō Shin and modelled on Shuri Castle, its balustrades carved with dragons, phoenixes and lions. A National Treasure as well as a UNESCO component.

rows.w: The Ryūkyū Kingdom's ceramics quarter: a 400 m stone-paved street between Kokusai-dōri and Route 330 lined with potteries, kilns and shops selling yachimun ware and shisa, with wheel-throwing classes.

rows.n: Shuri Castle (首里城)
rows.w: Palace of the Ryūkyū Kingdom from 1429 to 1879 and the centrepiece of the UNESCO Gusuku Sites. Destroyed in 1945 and again by fire in 2019; the rebuilt Seiden (main hall) exterior is complete, its interior due to reopen on 23 November 2026.

rows.n: Makishi Public Market (第一牧志公設市場)

rows.n: Shuri Ryusen bingata & coral-dye studio (首里琉染)
rows.w: Bingata workshop and shop five minutes' walk from Shuri Castle Park, selling bingata and its own 'coral-dye' (sango-zome) textiles. Upstairs visitors can try coral dyeing (about 50 minutes) and watch artisans dyeing in the third-floor studio.

rows.n: Kume Shiseibyō Confucius Temple (久米至聖廟)
rows.w: Naha's Confucian temple, a centre of Chinese learning for the Ryūkyū Kingdom since the original was built in 1671–75; its precinct holds the Meirindō, Okinawa's first public school. Rebuilt in Kume in 2013 beside Fukushū-en, on the old Chinese-émigré Kume village.

rows.n: Arakaki Family Residence, Tsuboya (新垣家住宅)
rows.w: The only surviving 18th-century Tsuboya potter's compound — red-tiled main house, workshop, climbing kiln (the former royal 'Higashi-nu-kama') and stone pigsty-toilet — designated an Important Cultural Property in 2002.

rows.n: Tsushima Maru Memorial Museum (対馬丸記念館)
rows.w: Museum (opened 22 Aug 2004) on the 1944 sinking of the evacuation ship Tsushima Maru, in which hundreds of Okinawan schoolchildren died; run by the Tsushima Maru Memorial Association beside Gokoku-ji and Naminoue.

rows.n: Heiwa-dōri Shopping Arcade (平和通り商店街)
rows.w: Covered arcade of around 200 shops branching off Kokusai-dōri toward Makishi Public Market, nicknamed the 'labyrinth arcade'. Named 'Peace Street' by public competition in 1951 after the Heiwa-kan cinema at its mouth; a new generation of shop owners has revived it since the 2000s.

rows.n: Naha City Museum of History (那覇市歴史博物館) — CLOSED
rows.w: Opened in 2006 to show the National Treasure 'Materials related to the Shō Family of Ryūkyū Kings' (1,166 documents and 85 art objects, including the royal crown). It closed on 31 August 2025; the treasures are due to be shown at the former Nakagusuku Udun site, opening date not yet set.
